mcqs.question: Without register renaming, why must an out-of-order engine still serialize instructions that only have a WAR or WAW hazard?
options: Because WAR/WAW hazards involve real data flowing between the instructions, just like RAW
Because the ALU can only process one register name per program run
Because both instructions share the same register name, and executing them out of order would leave the wrong final value in that register even though no value actually needs to pass between them
Because WAR/WAW hazards only occur in floating-point instructions
mcqs.explanation: WAR/WAW hazards are purely about register-name reuse, not data flow — but without renaming, the hardware has no way to tell that apart from a real dependence, so it must conservatively serialize. No value actually flows in WAR/WAW, unlike RAW, and the hazard isn't restricted to floating-point instructions.

mcqs.question: When two instructions both write architectural register R1, what does register renaming do?
options: It merges both writes into a single physical register to save space
It converts both instructions into no-ops
It delays the second write until the first is guaranteed to have committed
It allocates each write a different physical register from the pool, so the name collision that caused the WAR/WAW hazard no longer exists at the hardware level
mcqs.explanation: Renaming gives each write to the same architectural register a distinct physical register, eliminating the hazard entirely rather than working around it with delays. Merging into one register or turning instructions into no-ops would be incorrect and destroy the program's actual behavior.

mcqs.question: Which statement about what register renaming eliminates is correct?
options: Renaming eliminates WAR and WAW hazards but leaves true RAW dependences untouched — a genuine data value must still flow in order
Renaming eliminates RAW hazards entirely, since renamed registers never need to wait for a value
Renaming eliminates all three hazard types (RAW, WAR, WAW) equally
Renaming eliminates control hazards from branches
mcqs.explanation: Renaming only removes name-based conflicts (WAR/WAW); a RAW dependence is a real data requirement that renaming cannot make disappear — the consuming instruction still must wait for the actual value. Control hazards are a separate category handled by branch prediction, not renaming.

mcqs.question: What's the key difference between architectural register count and physical register count?
options: They are always the same number in every CPU
Architectural register count is fixed by the ISA and visible to software; physical register count is a microarchitecture implementation detail that can differ across chip generations of the same ISA
Physical register count is always smaller than architectural register count
Architectural registers are only used for floating-point values
mcqs.explanation: The ISA fixes the architectural register count as part of its instruction encoding, stable across all implementations, while physical register count is an internal design choice invisible to software and can vary between generations of cores implementing the same ISA. Physical count is typically much larger, not smaller, and architectural registers aren't limited to floating-point.
